feed.title: Wits AHEAD · Daily briefing
feed.subtitle: News, research, video and readings on AI, data and human capability in higher education, curated every morning.
feed.rights: Wits AHEAD Research Group, Wits School of Education, University of the Witwatersrand

entry.title: South Africa must move from talking about AI to delivering for young job-seekers, Tshwane University of Technology dialogue hears
entry.summary:
IOL reports on the 5th Annual Future of Work Dialogue, hosted in Pretoria on 30 September and 1 October by Tshwane University of Technology's Institute for the Future of Work, which asked government, business, universities and labour to stop debating what AI might mean and decide who will deliver what, and by when. The backdrop is Statistics South Africa's Quarterly Labour Force Survey for the second quarter of 2026, which put youth unemployment at 47.4% (https://www.statssa.gov.za/?p=19804), and a split in attitudes: young people in work largely see AI as a boost, while an African Leadership University survey found that only 36% of school leavers saw AI as an opportunity for their career. Organisers called for faster curriculum change, more apprenticeships and workplace learning, and earlier signals from employers on emerging skills such as AI literacy, cloud computing, cybersecurity and data engineering.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 4, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, the dialogue names the gap Wits AHEAD studies: universities update curricula more slowly than employers change the skills they want, and AI risks widening the distance between young people in work and those still looking. Its call for a time-bound plan with named responsibilities is a test South African universities, Wits included, can be measured against.

IOL (Ronnie Xaba) · Established press report

entry.title: California law requires its public colleges and universities to set safety standards for buying AI and to train students and staff
entry.summary:
Governor Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 2392 on 30 September 2026, requiring the California Community Colleges and the California State University, and requesting the University of California, to convene a joint working group that will recommend, by 1 January 2028, standards for buying generative AI systems and training in their use. Any system procured must have a documented risk assessment, must not trade factual accuracy for flattering 'sycophancy', must collect only the data its educational purpose needs, and its vendor must disclose its training data sources, including whether student work was used. Until the standards exist, each systemwide AI contract must be reported to the state Legislature within 60 days, with an account of how the system was chosen.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, responsible AI, ethics and policy, this is one of the first laws to set what a university must demand of an AI vendor before signing, not after. Universities in the Global South, which often receive AI tools through donor or vendor deals, can borrow its checklist: risk assessment, data minimisation, disclosure of training data and public reporting of each contract.

California Legislature (Assembly Bill 2392, Chapter 855 of 2026) · State legislation (official bill text)

entry.title: A college president on harnessing AI in education without cutting corners
entry.summary:
Colby College president David Greene tells ABC News how the American liberal arts college is harnessing artificial intelligence in teaching and learning in a way he describes as ethical and that does not cut corners. It is a short, first-hand account of institutional leadership on AI.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 1, generative AI in higher education, it shows a university leader treating AI as something to shape deliberately rather than only to police, the stance Wits AHEAD argues for in African universities.

ABC News · ABC News (US national broadcaster)

entry.title: What should a university be in the age of AI? SABC News on the first Times Higher Education summit in Africa
entry.summary:
Ahead of the Times Higher Education World Academic Summit, hosted by the University of Cape Town from 29 September to 1 October and the first held on African soil, SABC News asks what a university should look like as AI changes how people work, learn and create knowledge. UCT's Deputy Vice-Chancellor for Research and Internationalisation, Prof Thokozani Majozi, discusses the summit's theme, "Knowledge, justice and futures: Universities in the age of intelligence", and the role of universities beyond producing graduates.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 4, graduate capability and transitions, the summit's question of what universities owe graduates and society as AI reshapes work is the group's own, now asked on a South African stage.

SABC News · SABC News (public broadcaster)

entry.title: African scholarship is building a decolonial agenda for AI in university classrooms, systematic review finds
entry.summary:
A systematic review in Trends in Higher Education maps 25 studies from 2010 to 2025 on decoloniality, artificial intelligence and university classrooms in African higher education. Output accelerated after 2020 around three themes, epistemic injustice and curriculum, algorithmic coloniality and data extractivism, and the teaching adaptations generative AI demands, with research concentrated in South Africa and emerging Pan-African work on African-language AI. The authors find a coherent decolonial AI research agenda taking shape, but little empirical evidence so far.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, responsible AI and policy, it names the questions of whose knowledge and whose languages AI carries into African classrooms, and shows how thin the empirical base still is, a gap research in the Wits School of Education can help fill.

Trends in Higher Education (MDPI) · Peer-reviewed systematic review

entry.title: AI emerges as a distinct part of the student academic experience in a survey of 2,403 Bolivian undergraduates
entry.summary:
A study of 2,403 undergraduates at a private university in Bolivia, published in Education Sciences, validates a 31-item survey of the academic experience and finds that students' reported use of AI in their learning forms a distinct factor alongside engagement, critical thinking, teaching quality and dedication. Reported AI use was positively associated with academic engagement and with communication, ethical and critical-thinking skills; the authors stress that the instrument measures perceptions, not learning outcomes.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 1, generative AI in higher education, a validated Global South instrument that treats AI use as part of how students experience university is a practical tool the group could adapt for South African student surveys, with the authors' caution that it measures perception, not learning.

Education Sciences (MDPI) · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Oxford let OpenAI train AI models on Bodleian Library texts, the Guardian reports
entry.summary:
Internal documents obtained by the Guardian show the University of Oxford has let OpenAI digitise historical material from its Bodleian Library, among them 125,000 scans of nineteenth and twentieth century doctoral theses and 10,000 Tudor-era broadside ballads, to help train its AI models. Oxford's 2025 partnership with OpenAI was announced as a project to widen access to rare texts; it did not disclose that the scans would feed OpenAI's training data. Staff minutes show governance-committee members raised concerns about reputational risk and the energy cost of AI, while Oxford says the material is modest in scale, out of copyright, and will be published openly online within months.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, responsible AI, ethics and policy, the episode is a caution for any university, in the Global South as much as Oxford, that lets an AI company handle its archives or data: without clear public disclosure of how material will be used, a genuine access project can look, in hindsight, like a quiet data-supply arrangement, which is exactly the transparency gap Wits AHEAD presses institutions to close before signing.

The Guardian (Ethan Penny and Dan Milmo) · Established press investigation

entry.title: University of Ghana approves an AI policy and a compulsory digital literacy course for every student
entry.summary:
The University of Ghana's Council has approved a university-wide policy on artificial intelligence, drawn up after a campus survey found gaps in training, limited access to AI tools and worries over accuracy, academic integrity and ethics. Announcing it at the university's congregation in Accra, where 1,884 students graduated, the vice-chancellor, Professor Nana Aba Appiah Amfo, said the university will also require every student, from the next academic year, to take a new Digital Literacy and Applied AI course, alongside a separate Teaching and Learning Policy.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 1, generative AI in higher education, a public university moving from guidance documents to a compulsory AI literacy course for every graduate, built on its own evidence of where students and staff are struggling, is the kind of structured, campus-wide response Wits AHEAD looks for across the continent, rather than policies that exist on paper alone.

University of Ghana (policy document); Ghanaian Times · University policy document

entry.title: OECD finds generative AI use nearly universal in higher education but only one in five institutions has a formal policy
entry.summary:
An OECD Education Spotlights report, Policies supporting responsible and systematic GenAI adoption in higher education, finds that generative AI use among university students has become nearly universal, rising from 66 per cent of UK undergraduates in 2024 to 95 per cent in 2026, with 86 per cent of students across a 16-country survey now using it. Yet only 19 per cent of higher education institutions worldwide had a formal generative AI policy in 2025, though a further 42 per cent were drafting one, and only 17 per cent of academic staff globally counted as advanced or expert users.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, responsible AI, ethics and policy, the gap the OECD measures, almost universal everyday use against formal governance in barely one institution in five, is precisely the gap Wits AHEAD was set up to help close, and a reminder that adopting AI tools and governing them responsibly are two different jobs that most universities have not yet finished either of.

University World News (Karen MacGregor), reporting an OECD report · Intergovernmental research report, reported by established press

entry.title: African universities urged to collaborate and use AI responsibly, Times Higher Education summit hears
entry.summary:
At the Times Higher Education World Academic Summit in Cape Town, the organisation's business development manager for sub-Saharan Africa, Mosebjadi Petje, called on African universities to share research infrastructure and expertise to tackle shared challenges such as climate change and youth unemployment, and to embrace artificial intelligence "responsibly" rather than resist it. He also urged institutions to use their own data for strategic decisions rather than for rankings alone, addressing delegates from the roughly 55 sub-Saharan African universities that feature in the Times Higher Education World University Rankings.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, a call from within the continent's own university sector for shared infrastructure and responsible AI use, rather than imported rules, speaks directly to the collaborative, Africa-led approach Wits AHEAD takes to AI governance in higher education.

Channel Africa (SABC international service) · Established broadcaster

entry.title: US unemployment rate for university graduates falls to 2.5%, lowest of any education group, official data show
entry.summary:
The United States Bureau of Labor Statistics reports that the unemployment rate for people with a bachelor's degree or higher fell to 2.5% in September 2026, down from 2.7% in August, remaining the lowest jobless rate of any education group the agency tracks. The release, USDL-26-1549, also shows unemployment for workers without a university qualification running several percentage points higher across the same month.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 4, AI, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, official US data showing the degree-holder unemployment gap widening again is a reminder that, even as AI reshapes entry-level hiring worldwide, a university qualification still carries a measurable labour-market premium that Wits AHEAD's own employability research is testing for the Global South.

US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Employment Situation News Release (September 2026) · National statistics office

entry.title: UCT vice-chancellor says all students will be trained to use AI, not banned from it
entry.summary:
Speaking at the Times Higher Education World Academic Summit in Cape Town, the University of Cape Town's vice-chancellor, Professor Mosa Moshabela, said the university has moved from restricting generative AI to training every student to use it responsibly, at different levels of complexity. UCT has stopped relying on AI detection tools to police student work and now treats AI, in his words, as "a partner in the teaching and learning project". The university is also working to make AI tools accessible beyond campus, since commercial tools remain unaffordable for many communities across the continent.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 1, generative AI in higher education, UCT's shift from policing AI use to training every student in it is the clearest sign yet that a major Global South university is treating AI literacy as a basic graduate competency rather than a disciplinary problem, a direction Wits AHEAD's own work on assessment and integrity tracks closely.

University of Cape Town News (story by Niémah Davids) · University announcement

entry.title: AI governance becomes higher education's top technology priority for the first time, EDUCAUSE survey finds
entry.summary:
EDUCAUSE, the US and Canadian higher education technology association, reports that its 2027 Top 10 IT Issues survey of 882 technology leaders placed determining where artificial intelligence adds real value at the top of the list for the first time, overtaking cybersecurity. Designing AI structures for responsible innovation and building a stronger data governance backbone also ranked in the top ten, drawn from the largest response pool the survey has recorded.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, the result shows AI governance has become higher education's central technology question across the Global North as well as the Global South, a shift Wits AHEAD's own policy work speaks to directly.

EDUCAUSE 2027 Top 10 IT Issues (via Campus Technology) · Higher education technology association survey

entry.title: University of Pretoria vice-chancellor says graduates need AI fluency and power skills, not just a degree, to find work
entry.summary:
Writing in Daily Maverick, University of Pretoria vice-chancellor Professor Francis Petersen argues that South African graduate unemployment persists alongside employer skills shortages because universities still prepare students for a single first job rather than a lifetime of career transitions. He says employers now expect graduates who can use AI proactively alongside communication, collaboration and critical thinking, and calls for internships, work-integrated learning and entrepreneurship support across every discipline.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 4, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, a South African vice-chancellor naming AI fluency as a core employability skill, alongside the power skills employers already demand, sharpens the case for Wits AHEAD's own work connecting analytics, curriculum and graduate outcomes.

Daily Maverick (Professor Francis Petersen, Vice-Chancellor, University of Pretoria) · University vice-chancellor opinion article, established press

entry.title: Bangladeshi university students show moderate knowledge but mixed practice on AI-assisted plagiarism, study finds
entry.summary:
A survey of 386 students at public and private universities in Bangladesh, published in the journal AI and Ethics, finds moderate knowledge and mixed practice regarding AI-giarism, the use of generative AI tools to produce work presented as a student's own, even though attitudes toward academic integrity were generally favourable. Attitudes differed significantly by university type, residential status, publication experience and discipline, and students with academic writing training reported better practice.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 1, generative AI in higher education, assessment and integrity, the finding that favourable attitudes do not guarantee sound practice is a reminder that AI literacy, not policy alone, is what protects assessment integrity, a question just as live for Wits AHEAD's Global South partners.

AI and Ethics (Noakhali Science and Technology University) · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Lisbon university combines early-warning alerts with compulsory AI literacy to protect first-year students, study finds
entry.summary:
A whole-institution case study of Iscte, the University Institute of Lisbon, published in Education Sciences, describes nine years of combining a rule-based early-warning system that flags at-risk first-year students with a critical AI-literacy course that is compulsory on one campus and optional on the other. The authors report that academic risk concentrates in identifiable groups and that a shared AI-literacy baseline is achievable, but that support reaches only a minority of flagged students and that predictive models trained on one cohort transfer poorly to the next.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 2, predictive analytics for student success, retention and early warning, the honest finding that support and prediction both have real limits is a useful caution for Wits AHEAD as it weighs its own early-warning tools against the resourcing needed to act on them.

Education Sciences (Iscte - University Institute of Lisbon) · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: OECD data show graduate unemployment rising for the first time since its records began
entry.summary:
The OECD's Education at a Glance 2026, launched on 29 September 2026, found that unemployment among 25 to 34 year olds with a university degree rose by 0.4 percentage points across member countries between 2023 and 2025, while unemployment among those with only upper secondary education fell by 0.2 percentage points, narrowing the usual gap and marking the first such reversal since the series began in 2000. South Korea illustrates the pattern starkly: 71.1% of its 25 to 34 year olds hold a tertiary qualification, well above the OECD average of 47.5%, yet its graduate employment rate of 80.1% trails the OECD average of 86%.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 4, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, this is the clearest OECD-wide signal yet that a degree's labour-market advantage is narrowing just as AI reshapes entry-level work, a trend Wits AHEAD should track against South Africa's own graduate destination data.

OECD, Education at a Glance 2026 (via UPI) · Intergovernmental body data, reported by an international wire service

entry.title: Côte d'Ivoire launches UNESCO-backed AI training for 3,000 vocational education teachers
entry.summary:
Côte d'Ivoire's Minister Delegate for Technical Education and Vocational Training, Jean-Louis Moulot, launched a programme on 25 September 2026 to train 3,000 vocational education teachers, pedagogical supervisors and administrators in artificial intelligence, with technical support from UNESCO. The first phase runs from 1 October to 30 December 2026, training 1,000 teachers in Abidjan in AI fundamentals, educational applications, assessment methods, ethics and data security, before the pilot is evaluated for nationwide expansion.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 3, AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education, this is a rare government-led, UNESCO-supported programme that trains the teacher-educators themselves rather than only their students, a model Wits AHEAD can draw on in its own work with South African technical and vocational colleges.

TrendsnAfrica · Government programme launch with UNESCO technical support, reported by regional press

entry.title: Ghana commits to train 100,000 TVET facilitators in AI under new UNESCO and Microsoft partnership
entry.summary:
Ghana's Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) Service signed a memorandum of understanding with UNESCO, KPMG and Microsoft on 30 September 2026 to train at least 100,000 TVET facilitators in artificial intelligence and digital skills under the AI EmpowerED initiative. TVET Service director general Dr Eric Kofi Adzroe said the partnership marked a shift towards a system aligned with industry, powered by technology and focused on outcomes, while UNESCO country representative Edmond Moukala signed the agreement on the organisation's behalf.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 4, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, equipping technical and vocational instructors with AI skills at this scale could reshape how an entire generation of African artisans and technicians enters an AI reshaped labour market, a model Wits AHEAD watches for lessons applicable to South Africa's own TVET sector.

Graphic Online · National press, government partnership announcement

entry.title: US learning platform data shows AI tools trail far behind other classroom technology
entry.summary:
Instructure's new EdTech Top 40 report, based on anonymised data from 19.5 million higher education users of its Canvas learning platform between September 2025 and April 2026, found that Google Gemini, the most widely adopted dedicated AI tool, reached only 87,788 users across 211 institutions and failed to crack the top 100 integrated tools. Established tools such as McGraw Hill, with 11.3 million users, Watermark course evaluations and Zoom remained far more widely used. Instructure vice-president Ryan Lufkin said universities were signing enterprise wide AI deals without yet embedding the tools into everyday coursework.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 1, generative AI in higher education, the gap between institutional AI licensing and actual classroom use is a caution Wits AHEAD is tracking: buying access to AI tools is not the same as integrating them into teaching and assessment, and the group's own work on practical adoption speaks directly to that gap.

Inside Higher Ed · Established press report on industry usage data

entry.title: UNESCO programme trains over 100 rural teachers and principals across China and Southeast Asia in AI and STEM
entry.summary:
UNESCO reported on 30 September 2026 that its China-Southeast Asia Capacity Development Programme for Teachers and Principals, held in Beijing from 17 to 23 August 2026 under the theme 'STEM and AI: Empowering Rural Teachers for Digital Transformation', brought together over 100 education policymakers, school leaders, teachers and experts from China and Southeast Asian countries. Organised with UNESCO's International Research and Training Centre for Rural Education, SEAMEO RECSAM, the UNESCO Chair on Artificial Intelligence in Education at Beijing Normal University and the OECD, the programme focused on using AI and STEM teaching to advance digital equity in underserved rural communities. Professor Shahbaz Khan, director of UNESCO's Regional Office for East Asia, called for 'human centred, ethical and inclusive AI in education'.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 3, AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education, the programme's insistence that technology can support but never replace rural teachers offers a model Wits AHEAD can draw on for its own work preparing teacher educators across under resourced parts of the Global South.

UNESCO · Intergovernmental body

entry.title: Ethiopia's Education Ministry says AI will support, not replace, teachers as it expands digital learning
entry.summary:
Ethiopia's Minister of Education, Berhanu Nega, said on 29 September 2026 that teachers across the country are being supported to use artificial intelligence for lesson preparation, content development, student support and assessment, alongside digitalisation of the ministry's Education and Higher Education Management Information Systems. The Minister stressed that AI is being introduced to strengthen teachers' capacity rather than replace them, as part of a wider push on online, blended and micro credential learning and stronger digital connectivity for universities and schools. He called for the education system to move beyond memorisation and develop critical thinkers who can 'work together with machines'.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 1, generative AI in higher education, and pillar 5, analytics and data for education systems, a national ministry publicly committing to AI as a support for teachers rather than a replacement, alongside systems level data reform, is the kind of policy signal Wits AHEAD tracks across the Global South.

allAfrica (Ethiopian News Agency) · National press, government ministry announcement

entry.title: Africa must build its own AI solutions rather than import them, says UN scientific panel member
entry.summary:
Girmaw Abebe Tadesse, who leads Microsoft's AI for Good Lab in Kenya and sits on the United Nations' Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence, told UN News during UN High Level Week in New York on 25 September 2026 that African countries should identify their own problems before adopting technology designed elsewhere. He said stakeholders, including higher education institutions, governments, development partners and technology companies, should pool knowledge to build solutions suited to local realities rather than duplicating effort, and pointed to Africa's young population as a source of innovation already applying technology to community challenges.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, a UN scientific adviser explicitly naming universities as essential partners in a locally led AI agenda reinforces the case for Wits AHEAD's own emphasis on African owned research and solutions, not imported frameworks.

allAfrica (UN News) · UN News Service, intergovernmental body

entry.title: Cape Town hosts first African THE World Academic Summit as Wits and four other South African universities rise in the world rankings
entry.summary:
The Times Higher Education World Academic Summit opened at the University of Cape Town on 30 September 2026, the first time the event has been held on the African continent, alongside the launch of the THE World University Rankings 2027. Five South African universities now rank in the global top 500, including Wits at 301 to 325, with the University of Cape Town rising to joint 147th, its best position in seven years. UCT vice-chancellor Mosa Moshabela said the university had switched off its AI detection tools to focus on teaching students to use AI properly, while Higher Education Minister Buti Manamela noted that six in ten young South Africans are unemployed.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 1, generative AI in higher education, UCT's decision to drop AI detection in favour of teaching proper use marks a shift in assessment policy that Wits AHEAD is tracking across the sector, and the rankings rise together with the Minister's unemployment figure underline why AI, analytics and graduate capability matter for every South African university, Wits included.

Daily Maverick · Established press

entry.title: Alliance for African Partnership meets in Dar es Salaam and puts AI skills at the centre of regional cooperation

category.term: Africa (Tanzania, hosted by the University of Dar es Salaam)

entry.summary:
The Alliance for African Partnership, a consortium of 12 universities from 10 African countries anchored by Michigan State University, held its 2026 annual meeting at the University of Dar es Salaam from 16 to 22 September. Deputy Vice-Chancellor for Research Nelson Boniface told delegates that universities must update their curricula and train lecturers so that graduates are not left behind by artificial intelligence, adding that AI literacy is now a skill every student needs, not only computer scientists.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 4, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, the Alliance's call for curriculum reform and lecturer training across ten African countries echoes Wits AHEAD's own case for embedding AI literacy in every discipline, not only STEM, to keep African graduates employable.

allAfrica.com, from the Daily News (Tanzania) · Established African news service

entry.title: Morgan State University wins 10 million dollar federal grant to build a trusted AI research institute
entry.summary:
Morgan State University, a historically Black university in Baltimore, has received 10 million dollars in United States federal funding to establish the Institute for Trusted Autonomous Networks, known as TITAN, US senators Chris Van Hollen and Angela Alsobrooks announced on 16 September 2026. The five year grant funds research and doctoral training in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and quantum enhanced security, and is intended to help Morgan State reach the highest tier of American research universities.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 3, AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education, TITAN's focus on training doctoral researchers at a historically Black university shows how targeted AI research funding can widen who leads AI research, a question Wits AHEAD tracks for equity in STEM worldwide.

CBS News Baltimore · Established press

entry.title: MIT trains faculty from other universities to teach AI across disciplines
entry.summary:
The MIT Stephen A. Schwarzman College of Computing has piloted a week long workshop that trains faculty from other colleges and universities to teach artificial intelligence and machine learning within their own subjects, adapting materials from MIT's own "Modelling with Machine Learning" course. The inaugural workshop in July 2026 brought together 19 academics from seven institutions, including Allen University, Babson College, Brandeis University and the University of Massachusetts at Lowell, with more than half a dozen MIT instructors teaching sessions spanning finance, computer science and sustainability.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 3, AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education, the pilot tackles a bottleneck Wits AHEAD also faces: academics outside computer science need practical, hands on training before they can teach AI literacy credibly within their own disciplines.

MIT News · University announcement

entry.title: UNESCO survey finds most Latin American and Caribbean universities use AI, but few have a strategy
entry.summary:
UNESCO's International Institute for Higher Education in Latin America and the Caribbean (IESALC), working with the United Nations University Institute for the Advanced Study of Sustainability, surveyed 200 higher education institutions across 19 countries and published its findings on 8 September 2026 during UNESCO's Digital Learning Week. It found that 87 per cent of institutions already use AI in at least one area of their work, most often in teaching and learning, but only 26 per cent have a formal AI strategy. Most AI initiatives start with individual academics, researchers or students rather than institutional leadership.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, the gap between near universal AI use and formal governance across Latin America and the Caribbean mirrors a pattern Wits AHEAD tracks across the Global South, where everyday practice is running ahead of institutional policy.

UNESCO IESALC and United Nations University · Intergovernmental higher education body report

entry.title: University of Colorado system adopts a living policy for responsible use of AI
entry.summary:
The University of Colorado system's new Administrative Policy Statement 6012, Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence, took effect on 24 August 2026 and was set out on the university's policy blog on 21 September. It establishes systemwide expectations for academic integrity, data protection, transparency and verifying AI-generated content for accuracy, and is explicitly presented as a policy meant to evolve as feedback comes in from students and staff.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 1, generative AI in higher education, teaching, assessment and integrity, a large public university system choosing to treat its AI rules as a living document rather than a fixed policy is a Global North comparator for the governance choices Wits AHEAD tracks in the Global South.

University of Colorado · University policy announcement

entry.title: University of Pretoria trains future teachers in "prompt literacy" for the AI classroom
entry.summary:
Researchers in the University of Pretoria's Department of Early Childhood Education, led by Dr Joyce West and Dr Kayla Willemse, are running a multi-phase study on prompt literacy, the ability to give generative AI clear instructions while critically judging what it produces. The project trains future teachers to use AI as a collaborative classroom tool rather than a threat, through activities such as building children's stories and digital materials, while keeping a close eye on bias, inaccuracy and copyright in what the AI generates.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 3, AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education, the study addresses a gap Wits AHEAD watches closely: whether new teachers are actually taught how to question AI output, not only how to produce it.

Future SA, reporting University of Pretoria research · South African higher education press, reporting university research

entry.title: East African universities and Arizona State University partner to build "AI-ready" higher education
entry.summary:
The Inter-University Council for East Africa, the East African Community's higher education body, announced a partnership on 9 September 2026 with Arizona State University's University Design Institute to help East African universities become AI-ready. The work covers four areas: leadership and governance, faculty development, research ecosystems and cross-institutional learning. The Design Institute brings experience from 26 countries and more than 140 institutions, including seven in Africa.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 5, analytics and data for education systems and decision-making, the partnership shows a regional higher education body building AI capacity across many universities at once, a model Wits AHEAD can compare against its own reach in Southern Africa.

Inter-University Council for East Africa · Intergovernmental higher education body announcement

entry.title: Maharashtra sets up a state committee to govern AI and data dashboards across its universities
entry.summary:
Maharashtra's Higher and Technical Education Department has issued a government resolution setting up an AI, Data Analytics and Dashboard Governance Committee, chaired by Professor Rajnish Kamat, vice-chancellor of Shivaji University, Kolhapur. Over its three-year term the nine-member committee must set a state AI strategy, choose priority uses for generative AI, machine learning and natural language processing, standardise data across the state's existing student, examination and scholarship dashboards, and build automated trend analysis and risk forecasting into a portal that currently only reports numbers, while meeting cybersecurity and privacy rules. It reports every quarter to the department's most senior civil servants.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 5, analytics and data for education systems and decision-making, this is one of the first state governments anywhere to put a standing, accountable committee in charge of turning a reporting dashboard into a genuine early-warning and decision-support system, a model Wits AHEAD can point to when arguing for the same shift in South Africa.

Government of Maharashtra, Higher and Technical Education Department · State government resolution, reported by regional press

entry.title: Telkom Foundation, BCX and Alibaba Cloud partner with Wits to give students AI-powered coding tools
entry.summary:
Telkom Foundation, BCX and Alibaba Cloud have partnered with the University of the Witwatersrand to give about 165 third-year Computer Science students access to Alibaba's Qoder AI-powered development platform for their academic software projects. The Qoder Programme is meant to give students hands-on experience of AI-assisted coding tools before they enter a workplace where such tools are now standard, and to strengthen the link between the Wits curriculum and industry practice. Professor Richard Klein, head of the Wits School of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics, said the curriculum needs to evolve alongside these global developments.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 4, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, this is a concrete step by Wits itself to close the gap between what computer science graduates learn and the AI-augmented software engineering roles they will enter, at a scale Wits AHEAD can track and build on.

Wits University · University announcement

entry.title: Systematic review of 124 studies finds AI's value in education depends on governance, not the technology, and flags a Global South research gap

category.term: Global (evidence base: Central Asia, East Africa)

entry.summary:
A systematic narrative review by researchers based at universities in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Tanzania synthesised 124 studies published between January 2020 and January 2026 on how artificial intelligence is reshaping education. It found a real but uneven shift from isolated AI tools towards more adaptive, data-informed teaching, and concluded that whether this shift helps or harms learners depends on governance and institutional context rather than the technology itself, and that human judgement and the teacher's role must stay central rather than treating AI as an autonomous authority. The authors also found the evidence base itself skewed heavily towards English-language scholarship, with Global South, indigenous and multilingual perspectives still largely missing.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, this is a peer-reviewed confirmation, from researchers themselves based in Central Asia and East Africa, of the exact evidence gap that motivates Wits AHEAD's own work: the literature meant to guide AI policy in education barely includes the Global South voices it should be guided by.

Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Business schools bring back oral defences as AI use rises
entry.summary:
Leading European business schools, among them Insead, Imperial College Business School and HEC Paris, are reintroducing oral defences, pen-and-paper exams and closely supervised assessment because generative AI has undermined the standard take-home case study. Imperial's Peter Todd said staff can no longer be confident what a written submission represents unless students defend it in person or write it under supervision, and HEC Paris now alternates between assessments done with computers and without them. The Graduate Management Admission Council said assessment standards need to be clearer if business qualifications are to keep their meaning.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 1, generative AI in higher education, this shows leading business schools abandoning take-home assessment altogether rather than patching it, which matters directly for how Wits AHEAD frames assessment integrity guidance for African universities facing the same pressure with far fewer resources for oral or supervised exams.

entry.title: African curriculum experts meet in Dar es Salaam to confront the AI challenge in teacher education
entry.summary:
The Sixth Conference of the African Curriculum Association was held in Dar es Salaam from 22 to 25 September 2026, bringing together curriculum developers, teacher trainers, researchers and policymakers from across the continent. Tanzania Institute of Education director general Dr Aneth Komba and ACA secretary general Dr Gertrude Namubiru led discussions on how African curricula and teacher preparation must adapt to artificial intelligence and rapid technological change while staying grounded in local skills and community needs. The conference set out to produce a Dar es Salaam Declaration on Education Transformation in Africa, aligned with the African Union's Agenda 2063 and the fourth Sustainable Development Goal.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 3, AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education, a continent-wide gathering setting out how teacher preparation itself must change for an AI-shaped classroom speaks directly to Wits AHEAD's work on what teacher educators need to know, not only what pupils and students should be taught.

entry.title: Universities must teach people to work ‘with AI, not for AI’, says King's College London head
entry.summary:
Speaking at the 2026 Korea Times Global Conference in Seoul, King's College London vice-chancellor Shitij Kapur said universities must ensure people work with artificial intelligence rather than for it. He set out five responsibilities for universities: redefining what learning means, preparing graduates for a changing labour market, protecting thoughtful scholarship, advancing AI for the collective good and making sure the technology strengthens rather than replaces human capability. Kapur argued that AI's development is not fixed, and that universities and nations can still shape how it is built and used rather than simply accepting it from the technology industry.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, a leading vice-chancellor putting universities at the centre of shaping AI rather than merely reacting to it supports Wits AHEAD's own case that higher education in the Global South should help set the terms of AI adoption, not just absorb tools built elsewhere.

entry.title: Latin America's universities embrace AI faster than they can govern it, new study finds
entry.summary:
A UNESCO IESALC study of 200 higher education institutions across 19 Latin American and Caribbean countries found that 87 per cent already use artificial intelligence in some part of their work, yet only 26 per cent have any formal AI framework. Adoption is highest among private non-profit universities, at 84 per cent, against 68 per cent for public institutions and 52 per cent for private for-profit providers, and 55 per cent of universities overall have no dedicated AI budget. UNESCO's Borhene Chakroun said maximising the benefits depends on sustained investment in access and capacity, with governance that ensures ethical use, transparency and accountability.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, this shows the gap Wits AHEAD warns against taking hold at scale: public universities, which serve the students with fewest alternatives, are adopting AI fastest in the classroom while lagging furthest behind on governance, training and funding to use it responsibly.

Times Higher Education · Established higher education press, reporting a UNESCO IESALC study

entry.title: African universities can drive talent development at scale, Mastercard Foundation tells Accra convening
entry.summary:
At the inaugural Higher Education Transformation Convening in Accra on 22 September 2026, the Mastercard Foundation's Dr John Nkengasong described African universities as 'engines of prosperity' and human capital infrastructure that must align teaching with labour markets and industry. The event recognised five institutions with the Africa Higher Education for Transformation (AHEFT) Prize: Addis Ababa University, 2iE, Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Muni University and the University of Rwanda. The foundation restated its goal of helping 30 million young Africans, 70 per cent of them women, into dignified work by 2030.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 4, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, a major funder framing universities as talent infrastructure, while naming AI as a force reshaping work, strengthens the case for Wits AHEAD's evidence on which graduate capabilities actually lead to dignified work in African labour markets.

University World News · Established higher education press

entry.title: 'Syncopathy' and AI: African HE must choose verification
entry.summary:
Writing in University World News, Dr Kende Kefale of the University of Cape Town coins 'syncopathy' for AI outputs, such as citations and arguments, that look plausible but skip verification, and argues that universities share the same flaw because checking work is costly and invisible while output is cheap and easy to count. He proposes that institutions disclose how much work receives human examination before credentials are conferred, that every automated detection system have a named person accountable for its errors, and that verification records become a lasting institutional output. He points to South Africa's draft National AI Policy, withdrawn in April 2026 after fabricated citations were found in its reference list.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar 6, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, the argument gives Wits AHEAD a practical frame for AI governance in African universities, one that places the cost of verification and accountability for automated judgements with institutions rather than with students.
